title: Opportunities and risks of large language models in psychiatry
study_design: Narrative review/commentary on opportunities and risks of large language models in psychiatry and mental health
population: Not a single study sample; discusses patients, clinicians, healthcare systems, and general population mental health
country_or_setting: General/global; examples include US healthcare and social media studies, NYU Langone Health System, and clinical mental health settings
ai_type_application: Large language models (LLMs); therapy chatbots; clinical decision support; natural language processing of clinical notes; predictive analytics; personal assistants
ai_exposure_intervention: Use or deployment of LLMs in psychiatric care, mental health support, clinical documentation, prediction, decision support, and conversational applications
comparator_control_group: Not applicable for the review itself; some cited primary studies include waitlist controls, clinician comparison, or unaugmented vs augmented LLMs
mental_health_outcome: Depression, anxiety, emotional distress, avoidant coping, empathy, loneliness/social connection, psychiatric functioning, suicide risk, broader population mental health and well-being
outcome_measurement_tool: Not applicable for the review itself; cited studies mention clinical and behavioral assessments, functional neuroimaging, psychiatric functioning assessments, health records-based prediction, and self-reported depression symptoms
positive_effects: Potential improved access to care, personalized support, efficient data collection, diagnostic support, treatment planning, monitoring, administrative streamlining, clinical note generation, therapy chatbot delivery of evidence-based interventions, improved problem-solving skills and reduced depression/anxiety in some pilot work, potential enhancement of empathy, support for research question generation
negative_effects_harms: Potential labor substitution with downstream mental health harms, privacy/data leakage concerns, bias and stereotype reinforcement, misinformation/hallucinations, inappropriate or unstable outputs, misinterpretation of nuanced symptoms, overreliance by clinicians, mismatch of values, reduced human-to-human socialization, possible worsening distress in vulnerable users, inequitable access to fine-tuned systems, limited transparency, cultural/regional limitations
evidence_type: Narrative review drawing on cited empirical studies, examples, and conceptual/regulatory frameworks
main_finding: LLMs may offer important benefits for psychiatric care and mental health research, but current evidence also identifies substantial ethical, clinical, social, and safety risks; responsible guardrails, red-teaming, oversight, and evaluation frameworks are needed before broad deployment.
effect_size_key_result: Review does not provide a pooled effect size. It cites examples such as GPT-4 identifying an optimal next-step antidepressant about 3/4 of the time, contraindicated or suboptimal options appearing in nearly half of vignettes in one study, augmented bipolar-depression prompting doubling expert-aligned choices with contraindicated/less preferred options in about 1 in 10 vignettes, and a pilot RCT reporting modest reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms with LUMEN versus waitlist.
limitations_bias: This is not a systematic review or meta-analysis; no formal risk-of-bias assessment reported; evidence base is early and heterogeneous; many claims are conceptual or based on small pilot studies and illustrative examples; cited LLM studies may have unstable prompting sensitivity and limited generalizability; regulation and long-term surveillance remain underdeveloped.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as background/context on AI effects on mental health and psychiatry, including both beneficial and harmful pathways, but not primary causal evidence on mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful contextual review for identifying mechanisms, risks, and candidate primary studies, but not itself a primary study estimating AI effects on mental health.
notes_for_research_question: The paper is highly relevant for framing pathways by which AI/LLMs could affect mental health: direct therapeutic effects, clinician support, social substitution, labor-market impacts, bias/privacy harms, and system-level consequences. It also highlights the need to distinguish personal-use AI effects from clinical AI deployment effects.
